categorias.pregunta_en: Is it raining more or less than before?
Is the land getting greener or browner?
categorias.descripcion_en: Satellite observations can help identify changes in forest condition, land cover and habitat. Ask whether a greenness change persists across years and whether it coincides with disturbance or land-use change.

categorias.pregunta_en: Are lakes and soils holding more or less water?
categorias.descripcion_en: Satellite radar can map water extent, while SWOT measures water-surface elevation. Changes can reflect seasonal inflows, evaporation and water management.

categorias.descripcion_en: Storm tracks from NOAA IBTrACS since 1981, counting every storm whose centre passed within about 150 km of a box around Nicaragua, from the Caribbean or the Pacific.

investigaciones.definicion_en: Water in the top 10 cm of soil, from a land model.

fuente.producto: NASA GLDAS-2.1 Noah land model (GES DISC), regional mean

notas: Area-weighted average of the 0.25° GLDAS grid cells inside Nicaragua; cells the model treats as water are left out.
Grid cells with data cover at least 97% of the region's area.
Downloaded from NASA GES DISC (OPeNDAP) on 2026-11-14.
Rain minus evapotranspiration minus runoff should equal the change in stored water; over 2001–2024 it averages less than 2% of the rain, so the model's water budget adds up.

The GLDAS-2 documentation warns that its sunlight input shifted after 2011 and was rescaled from 2008, so a jump in 2008–2013 may come from the model's inputs rather than the climate. Compare with SMAP and MERRA-2 before reading a trend.

pasos.texto_en: Start with what NASA satellites measured: yearly rainfall over Nicaragua since 2001.
The slope is negative, but its 95% confidence interval includes zero: the record cannot tell a trend apart from year-to-year swings.
A second opinion: gauge-based datasets reach the same verdict.
Not significant does not mean no change. A longer record could make the same change detectable.
A longer record: rain gauges and satellites since 1981. Total yearly rain over Nicaragua: not enough evidence of a trend.
Year-to-year swings are large, and El Niño explains part of them. The notes show the result with El Niño removed.
How often it rains hard is another question. Days with at least 10 mm: −2.19 days/decade, trend detected. Since 2001 only: −0.183 days/decade, not enough evidence of a trend.
On the Caribbean coast, the wettest 5-day spell of each year: +9.05 mm/decade, trend detected. Since 2001 only: +18.2 mm/decade, methods disagree. The largest was in 2018.
2026: 589 mm from 1 January to 30 September, −43% compared with 1991–2020 and the driest of 46 years. That is an El Niño year.
Why a record-dry year does not make a trend on its own.
